goal:
Roll out 0.2.x runners and run fleet before/after interrupt recount (S5).

Source research: task 2e663986-aaf3-4afe-8dcf-3adad34acdb4 ("noticing a high level of interruptions"). Read docs/tasks/2e663986-aaf3-4afe-8dcf-3adad34acdb4/RESPONSE.md, docs/tasks/2e663986-aaf3-4afe-8dcf-3adad34acdb4/WIDE_NET_ANALYSIS.md, docs/tasks/2e663986-aaf3-4afe-8dcf-3adad34acdb4/TDD-TEST-EXAMPLES.md and the cited GUIDE before coding. Survey answers (if any) live in docs/tasks/2e663986-aaf3-4afe-8dcf-3adad34acdb4/RESPONSE_SURVEY.md. Section: RESPONSE.md S5, docs/tasks/2e663986-aaf3-4afe-8dcf-3adad34acdb4/GUIDE-05-commit-push-crash-loop.md (E5 sweep), WIDE_NET Cause 5 + rollout. Survey: q9 (gradual rollout, never force-restart mid-task). Ops + verification, no new unit tests.

Evidence: "Deployed runners are 0.1.0 (main f430f53, 11-11); repo is 0.2.0 with interrupt reasons and deterministic-git-failure handling (046a6391, merged 11-21 09:38 in 7ac148ce). Rollout is backend-nudged, at most daily per runner, idle-converge (docs/runner-update-runbook.md), so lag is expected - but until it lands, every new interrupt is still bare and every commit-hook rejection still crash-loops."

Steps: (1) confirm local-alpha + server2-alpha converge to build containing 046a6391 per docs/runner-update-runbook.md; record GET /runners versions before/after. (2) re-run WIDE_NET_ANALYSIS.md section 2 counts + GUIDE-07 section 5 fleet script: bare interrupts -> ~0, reasons name Causes 1/3/4, deterministic commit failures surface as FAILED with gitFailure payloads, never interrupts. (3) E5 forensics sweep (GUIDE-05 section 4): for each remaining post-finished interrupt, check kb-<taskId> worktrees (158394ab, db49d6c6, 1cae113f, 7f6220c3) for stage-output-commit presence (present -> Cause 2/4 territory; absent -> Cause 5). Only if E5 finds commit-loop cases 046a6391 does not cover, create a NEW Cause-5 code ticket. (4) record post-rollout counts in task folder as new baseline for S1-S4.

RISK: observe only - do NOT force-restart runners mid-assignment (PROD-ACTION, would create the interrupts being measured). Runs parallel to all code work; only prod CONFIRMATION of S3/S4/S2-runner-half waits on it.

- If a stage fails, put the reasoning in the FAIL block's reason and fix

- A FAIL block is honoured only with BOTH reason and fix guidance non-empty.

  treated as a pass and flagged for human review instead.

docs/runner-update-runbook.md
# Runner update runbook

Operator procedures for the runner self-update channel (Option A,
`docs/adr/0012-runner-artifact-update-channel.md`): cutting releases,
rolling back, migrating hosts to the wrapper, and triaging a runner
that says out of date. The backend directs version selection but never
serves runner bytes (R05) — every procedure below preserves that.

## Cutting a runner release (normal path)

The tag is the version source of truth; the pipeline cuts it.

1. Bump `runnerVersion` in `runner/version.json` (plain semver for
   fleet releases, e.g. `0.2.0`; suffixed tags like `0.3.0-rc.1` for
   canaries — v1 runners skip pre-releases automatically).
2. If the release needs a newer backend API, update the
   `requires.backendApi` range in the same file (e.g.
   `>=1.0.0 <2.0.0`). The release builder refuses manifests without a
   compat claim, and runners filter on this range.
3. Merge to the main line through the normal review flow.
4. Publish the runner (`publish.sh` with the runner component). The
   publish cuts and pushes the annotated `runner-vX.Y.Z` tag, which
   triggers `runner-release.yml`: full update-channel test gate, four
   platform archives, signed `manifest.json` + `.minisig`, GitHub
   release. Re-publishing an unchanged runner is a no-op success (the
   tag already exists, so nothing is re-cut).
5. Raise `KAINBAIN_RUNNER_RECOMMENDED_VERSION` to the new version on
   the backend. That is the one managed place: trailers light the
   "update available" badge and the backend auto-nudges command-capable
   ones (`requestUpdate`, at most daily per runner). Runners converge
   on idle with no SSH. Leave `KAINBAIN_RUNNER_MIN_VERSION` alone
   unless this is a breaking release (the 409 floor stops dispatch).

## Cutting a runner release (emergency path)

When the pipeline cannot cut the tag (CI down, urgent patch), tag by
hand from the release commit — the same builder runs:

```
git tag -a runner-vX.Y.Z -m "Runner runner-vX.Y.Z" <full-sha>
git push origin runner-vX.Y.Z
```

Then follow step 5 above. Never move an existing tag: cut a patch
version forward instead.

## Rollback drill (bad release, no host access needed)

1. Delete (or un-publish) the bad GitHub release so `releases/latest`
   resolves to the prior tag.

   platform archives, signed `manifest.json` + `.minisig`, GitHub
   release. Re-publishing an unchanged runner is a no-op success (the
   tag already exists, so nothing is re-cut).
5. Raise `KAINBAIN_RUNNER_RECOMMENDED_VERSION` to the new version on
   the backend. That is the one managed place: trailers light the
   "update available" badge and the backend auto-nudges command-capable
   ones (`requestUpdate`, at most daily per runner). Runners converge
   on idle with no SSH. Leave `KAINBAIN_RUNNER_MIN_VERSION` alone
   unless this is a breaking release (the 409 floor stops dispatch).

## Cutting a runner release (emergency path)

When the pipeline cannot cut the tag (CI down, urgent patch), tag by
hand from the release commit — the same builder runs:

```
git tag -a runner-vX.Y.Z -m "Runner runner-vX.Y.Z" <full-sha>
git push origin runner-vX.Y.Z
```

Then follow step 5 above. Never move an existing tag: cut a patch
version forward instead.

## Rollback drill (bad release, no host access needed)

1. Delete (or un-publish) the bad GitHub release so `releases/latest`
   resolves to the prior tag.

## Migrating a host to the wrapper

Direct `node main.js` units re-exec the same old directory on every
restart, so staged updates can never boot there. The migration lays a
versioned install root from the running tree and repoints the unit at
the stable wrapper shim — onto the SAME version (no update is staged,
so the fleet version does not change).

Per host, idle runners first; drain busy runners, then migrate:

```
# 1. Pre-check (read-only, safe any time):
KAINBAIN_RUNNER_INSTALL_ROOT=$HOME/.kainbain/runner-install \
  /path/to/runner/bin/kainbain-runner doctor --unit kainbain-runner-<id>.service

# 2. Rehearse:
scripts/migrate-runner-to-wrapper.sh --id <id> --dry-run

# 3. Migrate (snapshots unit + env, reloads, restarts, re-verifies):
scripts/migrate-runner-to-wrapper.sh --id <id>
```

The script refuses to overwrite an existing `current` link and prints
revert commands (copy the `.bak-<timestamp>` files back, reload,
restart). New installs need no migration: both installers
(`scripts/install-local-runner.sh`, `startRunner.sh`) already write
wrapper-based units. Verify after: `doctor` reports `status: ok` with
`entrypoint: wrapper`, and the next heartbeat shows the same version
as before.

## Restart vs Update (Settings › Runners)

Two separate actions, never combined:

- **Restart** reboots the runner on its **current version** — no update
  check runs. It is destructive: any work running on that runner is
  stopped at once (the claim lease expires so the work re-queues, like a
  crash). The confirm window names the runner and warns about running
  work; use it when a runner looks stuck, not to change versions.
  Mechanism: the daemon writes a `restart-requested` sentinel beside the
  install root and exits 0; the wrapper consumes it and boots the SAME
  tree again. Restart therefore needs the wrapper entrypoint — a runner
  started as bare `node main.js` exits without rebooting (migrate to the
  wrapper, above).
- **Update** reinstalls the runner onto its **target version** — the
  exact pin when the runner is pinned, otherwise the newest compatible
  release — and applies only when the runner is idle (never interrupts
  work). A busy runner queues the update for the next idle point.

## Per-runner version setting

Each runner is set to **Latest** (default) or one exact release, via
the version dropdown on its Settings › Runners detail panel:

- **Latest** tracks the newest release. It auto-updates at the next
  idle point (including right after a restart, once idle), and the
  backend nudges trailing runners at most daily. A red banner appears
  whenever a newer version exists than the one running — update (or
  wait for idle) to converge it.
- **Pinned** stays on exactly that release. Pinned runners never
  auto-update (no nudges, no idle installs, no restart-time installs);
  only the manual **Update** button installs the pin, and only when the
  pin is newer than the running version — the channel never downgrades,
  so a pin older than running shows a softer warning and the Update
  button stays disabled with the reason. Pick Latest or a newer pin to
  move forward.

The dropdown lists Latest plus every fleet-known release (newest
first): each runner's running version plus the fleet recommended and
minimum knobs — offline-safe, no release catalogue fetch.

## Triage: a runner says out of date

Start on the runner host (or ask the host owner to run it) — the
doctor is read-only and never writes:

```
$KAINBAIN_RUNNER_INSTALL_ROOT/bin/kainbain-runner doctor --unit kainbain-runner-<id>.service
```

Match the Settings › Runners badge to a cause:

- **"update available" that never clears.** The runner trails
  `KAINBAIN_RUNNER_RECOMMENDED_VERSION` (Latest runners) or its pin.
  If the doctor says `entrypoint: direct`, migrate to the wrapper
  (above) — staged updates can never boot there. If the env shows
  `KAINBAIN_RUNNER_AUTO_UPDATE=0` (or `(unset)` with a host-level
  opt-out), the runner acked the nudge with "skipped: auto-update is
  disabled" — flip that switch. If the runner is pinned, only the
  manual Update button installs (pins never auto-update); a pin older
  than running refuses with "never downgrades" — pick Latest or a
  newer pin. If the recommended knob sits above every published
  release, lower it to the newest release. Otherwise the runner is
  likely just busy: it converges at the next idle check, or press
  Update now (idle-only, never interrupts work). Restart does NOT
  clear this — Restart reboots the same version.
- **"restart queued" that never clears / restart loop.** The runner
  collects `requestRestart` on every heartbeat but never reboots:
  check the journal for the `Runner restarting` line. If the line is
  there but no reboot follows, the runner is not supervised by the
  wrapper (bare `node main.js` exits instead of rebooting — migrate to
  the wrapper, above) or the install root is unwritable (look for
  `sentinel not written`). A `restart-requested` file left behind by a
  crash causes at most one extra boot on the next clean exit — the
  wrapper consumes it, never loops. Old runners that predate the
  command show a disabled Restart with "too old" guidance instead —
  update them manually.
- **"below minimum" / 409 loop.** The runner is under
  `KAINBAIN_RUNNER_MIN_VERSION` and dispatch refuses it. It
  self-updates immediately when idle (interval bypassed). If it
  spins, check the journal for `Runner update` lines and treat the
  reason like an "update failed" below.
- **"update failed".** The next heartbeat carries `updateStatus`
  (`state: failed`, `reason`, `at`) — the badge tooltip shows it.
  Map the reason prefix: signature/key failure (release not signed
  by the pinned key — never hand-edit
  `PINNED_RELEASE_PUBLIC_KEY` in `runner/updates/verify.js` for a
  cut release); sha mismatch (re-download on next check); no asset
  for this platform (release is missing this host's tarball);
  incompatible with this backend (no newer release admits this
  backend's API — expected while the backend lags the release
  line); update lock held (a previous updater is still running or
  crashed mid-apply — stale locks self-heal); opted out (see
  above). Any failure keeps the old version running; fix the cause
  and the next idle check retries.
- **"rolled back" in the doctor.** Three crashed boots flipped
  `current` back to `previous`. Do not retry blindly: read the
  journal for the crash, fix forward with a patch release, and run
  the rollback drill above if the release is bad fleet-wide.

Backend-side checks: `KAINBAIN_RUNNER_MIN_VERSION` and
`KAINBAIN_RUNNER_RECOMMENDED_VERSION` values, the fleet matrix row
for the runner (`runnerVersion`, `updateAvailable`, `belowMinimum`,
`updateStatus`), and whether a `requestUpdate` command is pending or
was acked within the last 24h (the auto-nudge cooldown).

description: On an explicit planning request, always call `muse.read_skill` for this skill before answering. Research first, then return one concise inline plan; do not create a plan file unless the user explicitly asks or a governing workflow requires one. # Plan

Create a grounded, decision-complete plan before complex work.

## Scope

- How this body reached you decides whether this turn plans — the task text
  after it does not. When this body arrived inside your user message (the host
  expanded an explicit `/plan`, `/skill plan`, or "plan this" invocation), that
  invocation IS the explicit planning request: plan the subject named after it
  and stop at the plan, however small or implement-shaped that subject looks. Do
  not re-classify implement-shaped task text as an implement request — the user
  already chose planning by invoking. The use/skip trigger test in the bullets
  below applies only when you loaded this body yourself via `muse.read_skill` or it
  arrived as preloaded standing instructions.
- Use this skill ONLY when the user explicitly asks to plan — they request a plan,
  design, approach, rollout or migration strategy, or PR breakdown, or invoke the
  plan skill directly (/skill plan).
- Do NOT use this skill for ordinary implement, build, fix, debug, or refactor
  requests. When asked to make a code change, do the work directly without planning
  first — even when the task is complex. Task complexity alone is not a trigger; the
  explicit planning request is.
- Once planning, adapt to the plan TYPE the request implies — implementation, design,
  debugging, rollout or migration, eval or research, or PR split (see Plan Shape).
  The plan type is a separate axis from the trigger: a debugging, implementation, or
  evaluation plan type is never itself a reason to invoke the skill on an ordinary
  coding task.
- An explicit invocation (`/plan`, `/skill plan`, "plan this") always ends in a
  plan and never in the change itself, however small the change: a user who
  types `/plan` for a one-line edit wants the plan, not the edit. Only when the
  skill was offered automatically, skip it for simple one-step edits, obvious
  bug fixes, formatting, copy changes, and direct questions that can be
  answered without planning.
- Treat this as planning guidance, not a host-enforced mode. Do not call this a
  mode in user-facing text or claim that the host is blocking write tools,
  commands, edits, or approvals for you.
- Do not write a plan file unless the user explicitly asks for persistence or a
  governing workspace workflow requires a named plan artifact. You may write at
  most one such markdown file.
- Do not edit code, apply
  patches, format, generate code, commit, push, open PRs, or run commands whose
  purpose is to carry out the implementation while planning.
- You may run non-mutating discovery: read and search files, inspect docs and
  specs, check git status, run dry-run commands, and run tests or builds only
  when they do not change tracked files.
- Resolve facts that can be discovered locally before asking the user.
- Ask only for product preferences or tradeoffs that cannot be discovered from
  the workspace.

## Research Before Drafting

For an explicit plan, follow these steps in order. Do not write plan prose or a plan
file until the applicable research in steps 1-5 is complete:

1. **Map the decisions.** Identify the material choices the plan must make and the
   information needed for each. Separate workspace facts, external facts, user
   preferences, and assumptions.
2. **Research workspace facts.** Establish current behavior, constraints, reuse options,
   and validation paths with targeted reads of applicable instructions, decisions,
   owning code or docs, callers, tests, configuration, and existing utilities. Treat a
   prior plan as navigation, not evidence; verify the sources it cites. When the
   request pins a base commit or branch the checkout is not on, read files at that
   revision (`git show <rev>:<path>`, `git grep <pattern> <rev>`), not from the
   working tree, which holds another version.
3. **Ask only when necessary.** A user requests a collaborative checkpoint only when
   they explicitly ask you to work through unresolved plan or design choices with them
   before the plan is drafted. Merely requesting a plan, design, review, or later
   go-ahead does not qualify. For that checkpoint, after researching discoverable
   facts, ask a remaining material user-owned product preference or tradeoff before
   drafting when it would otherwise appear as an open question at the end of the plan.
   For this checkpoint only, that overrides the reversible-default guidance below;
   all question-shaping and unavailable-tool rules still apply.
   Otherwise follow the ordinary rule below. Before using a question tool, research any
   factual unknown that could eliminate the question; this may include bounded,
   preference-independent external research. Do not ask merely because scope, platform,
   or experience is unspecified. Ask only when a remaining
   user-owned preference cannot be resolved from the request, workspace, or research and
   its answer would materially change the research or recommendation, or avoid substantial
   rework. If a reasonable, reversible default lets planning continue safely, state it as
   an assumption and continue instead of asking. Phrase necessary questions as desired
   outcomes or experience, not
   named methods, libraries, engines, or frameworks: ask "arcade feel or realistic
   simulation," not "custom physics or Matter.js." Research and recommend the technical
   implementation yourself. When input is necessary, ask only one necessary question per
   turn. Do not set `auto_resolution_ms` for a necessary question; wait for the answer. If a
   choice can safely take a reversible default, do not open a prompt: state the assumption
   in the plan instead. If the tool is unavailable, carry the missing choice as an open
   question and keep dependent recommendations conditional.
   Prefer `request_user_input_async` when offered.
   If only `muse.request_user_input` is offered, use it and preserve its waiting and timeout behavior.
   An `accepted` result is neither a user answer nor approval.
   Use `auto_resolution_ms` only with `muse.request_user_input`.
   Continue independent work while awaiting an answer.
4. **Research external facts when they matter.** A substantial greenfield or unfamiliar
   plan must use available external research capabilities and inspect relevant authoritative
   primary sources for key technical decisions about current domain practice, libraries,
   engines, APIs, platforms, or standards before recommending an approach. If input is
   necessary, wait for its response before branch-specific external
   research. Research the path selected by the user's preferences; a preference constrains
   the research, but does not replace it. Source discovery is not source inspection. Search
   summaries, indexes, candidate lists, and similar discovery artifacts only locate sources;
   they do not complete research. Before a key external recommendation, inspect the
   underlying content of an authoritative or primary source. Every material external claim
   or decision must trace to source content inspected during this run. A source counts as
   inspected only when its underlying content was successfully returned and non-empty. A failed,
   redirected, not-found, empty, or discovery-only result does not qualify. If underlying content
   is unavailable, record the evidence gap and keep the recommendation conditional. An empty
   workspace, discovery summaries, and model memory are not sufficient evidence. Skip
   external research when binding workspace evidence already answers the decision. Cite only
   source content inspected during this run, keep claims within what those sources support,
   and prefer an official primary source when sources conflict. Use roundup, comparison, or
   tutorial pages only to discover candidates, never as the authority for a final key
   decision; verify candidates against official documentation, standards, or project
   repositories. Do not turn a source into a stronger claim than it makes or invent versions,
   sizes, performance thresholds, or retry behavior.
5. **Close delegated research.** Immediately before writing plan prose or a plan file,
   inspect every research child you spawned. A wait call timing out is not a terminal
   child state. While any child remains pending, check its status and keep waiting.
   Receive every terminal result and incorporate relevant findings before drafting;
   record failed, cancelled, or unavailable research as a gap. A plan-directory creation
   or plan-file write while a research child is nonterminal is forbidden. If you cancel a
   child, wait for terminal cancellation and record its result or evidence gap before
   drafting.
6. **Synthesize, then draft.** Immediately before drafting, build a private decision-evidence
   map. Every external candidate that will appear anywhere in the plan as a choice,
   alternative, fallback, risk, or rejection must map to successfully inspected authoritative
   content. Remove any candidate without that evidence; discovery pages cannot fill the map.
   Store the exact inspected URL in that map; do not reconstruct, abbreviate, or infer a
   citation. Only then recommend the approach. Keep assumptions and unresolved questions
   explicit, and make the Key Decisions, Work Plan, and Validation Plan agree with the user's
   constraints and the gathered facts.

Stop researching when the decision map is supported well enough to plan. Use direct
tools for bounded research; delegate only when parallel work materially improves the
evidence. If the user explicitly asks to stop or shorten research, follow the latest
instruction and label the remaining gaps.

## Quality Bar

A plan is ready only when it is:

- **Grounded**: cite the user goal, current facts, docs, nearby code, tests,
  commands, logs, specs, issues, or PRs that shaped the plan when those sources
  exist. Mark guesses as assumptions.
- **Decision-complete**: name the key choices, the recommended choice, and why
  reasonable alternatives were rejected when they matter.
- **Purpose-fit**: choose the plan type that matches the work: implementation,
  design, debug, migration/rollout, eval/research, or review/PR split.
- **Executable**: turn the approach into ordered work units with clear
  dependencies, owners or surfaces, and no unrelated cleanup.
- **Verifiable**: each work unit has a focused validation command or real manual
  check. Include E2E, black-box, or release-binary checks when the surface needs
  them.
- **Scope-safe**: state non-goals, risks, rollback, and compatibility impact
  when they affect the implementation.
- **Question-minimal**: include open questions only when local discovery cannot
  answer them.
- **Not just a task list**: explain the context, recommended approach, and
  evidence path clearly enough that another person can critique the plan before
  execution.

## Explicit File Output

Deliver the plan inline by default. Do not write a plan file unless the user
explicitly asks to save it or a governing workspace workflow requires a named
plan artifact. Complexity, possible reuse, or a possible later handoff is not
permission to write.

When persistence is authorized:

- If the user names a path, use it, even when a workflow or workspace convention would pick another; otherwise, if a governing workflow names one, use that path.
- With no named path, if the workspace has an established durable plan location, follow it. Prefer,
  in order: an active `specs/<feature>/plan.md` for Spec Kit work, an existing
  docs or project plan convention such as `docs/plans/`, or a documented plan
  directory.
- If saving and no stronger convention exists, save to `PLAN.md` at the
  workspace root — a visible project location. Do not default to
  `.agents/plans/`; use it only when the user or a governing workflow names it.
- Create parent directories as needed.
- You may update an active `specs/<feature>/plan.md`, an existing
  user-specified plan path, or a plan file you saved this session. Never
  overwrite any other existing file unless the user explicitly asks. When the
  root `PLAN.md` already exists and you may not overwrite it, save to
  `PLAN-<slug>.md` at the root instead. If that name is taken too, add a short
  numeric suffix (for example `PLAN-<slug>-2.md`).
- Do not use `/tmp` for the final plan. Temporary scratch is not a durable user
  artifact.

**File delivery.** When the user asks for the plan or design doc in a file, the
saved file is a delivery: after the readback audit, reply with a link to the
saved file, a one-line verdict, and the key decisions. Do not paste the plan
into the reply and do not add the `go` handoff lines; `go` still executes the
saved plan without regenerating it. If the user also says what the chat reply
should contain, reply only as they asked (the User-Visible Delivery exception
below). If the file cannot be saved, say so in one line and deliver the complete plan inline with the handoff instead.

## User-Visible Delivery

Exception: when the user asks for the plan in a file and also says what the chat reply should
contain (for example, just a one-line confirmation), the file is the delivery. Write the complete
plan to that file and audit it as Conversational Handoff requires, then reply only as the user
asked, with no handoff sentence at the start or end and no copy of the plan. The rule below that
saves a file only when the next reply can repeat it does not apply. A request that only asks for
the plan in a file does not trigger this exception; it follows the file-delivery rule in Explicit
File Output above.

Otherwise, start the final reply with these exact words on one line so the next action stays
visible even when a long plan is collapsed:

Here's the plan. I haven't made any changes yet. Reply `go` to start, or tell me what to adjust.

Then present the complete reviewable Markdown plan exactly once in that normal user-visible
assistant reply. Saving or rereading a plan file is not presenting it. When the user asked for
the plan in a file, presenting it is the link reply in Explicit File Output instead.

Use one canonical Markdown plan body. Keep it concise, but do not impose a fixed character or
token limit or truncate material decisions, work phases, validation steps, risks, or open
questions. Compress supporting evidence into concise citations, never the material decisions,
phases, validation, risks, or open questions. If you save a plan file, its content must be
exactly the canonical body. Copy the canonical body verbatim into the normal assistant reply, unless the user asked for the plan in a file.
Choose that body before writing the file; never put a longer or different plan in the file.
Save only when you can reproduce the entire exact body in the next normal reply, unless the
user asked for the plan in a file. If you cannot and no file was asked for, skip the file and
deliver the complete plan inline. Do not create two independently expanded
versions of the plan. If you save the plan, put its path after the visible plan; under the file-delivery rule the link reply replaces both. The saved file
is supplementary and never replaces the normal assistant reply, except under the exception
above and the file-delivery rule in Explicit File Output.
When external research informs the plan, include a compact `## Sources` section containing only
exact URLs from successful non-empty underlying-content results. Each material external decision
must cite one of those URLs.

## Conversational Handoff

Before delivery:

- Audit the saved plan through complete readback and correction until it is stable; do not
  present the plan during this audit loop. Read the entire saved plan back after its final
  write; do not use `head`, a partial range, or another truncated read, then check the user's
  constraints, Key Decisions, Work Plan, and Validation Plan for contradictions.
- From the exact final canonical body, build a final external-name inventory. Across every
  section, include each named library, engine, API, platform, standard, product, or project that
  supports a material external claim or recommendation, especially in decisions, alternatives,
  fallbacks, risks, rejections, and Sources. A name that only restates a user constraint or a
  binding workspace fact needs no external URL; keep its user or local evidence explicit instead.
  Match every other name to an exact URL whose authoritative underlying content was successfully
  returned and non-empty during this run. Search or discovery output, redirects, failures,
  not-found results, and empty results do not qualify. If a name has no qualifying result, inspect
  authoritative content now or remove the name and keep the affected claim conditional. Do not
  deliver until every inventory entry is resolved.
- Audit each material external decision against its matched source. Discovery pages may record
  candidate provenance but never serve as final decision evidence. Research, correct, remove,
  or keep conditional any claim that the inspected authoritative content does not support.
- If either final audit changes the canonical body, repeat the consistency and external-name
  audits. When a file is saved, rewrite it and read the entire saved plan again first. Deliver
  only after one complete pass makes no changes.
- Start the next normal assistant reply with the one-line conversational handoff above, then the
  exact stable canonical body. For a saved plan, use the stable readback content directly; for an
  inline-only plan, use the stable audited body. Do not regenerate, shorten, summarize, or omit
  any part. Put the saved path, when one exists, after the complete body. Under the User-Visible
  Delivery exception, reply only as the user asked instead. Under the file-delivery rule,
  reply with the link, verdict and key decisions instead.

After delivery:

- Do not use question tools for the final handoff. They remain reserved for
  necessary pre-draft user-owned choices in Research step 3.
- After the canonical plan and any saved path, repeat: “Reply `go` to start, or tell me
  what to adjust.” Under the User-Visible Delivery exception or the file-delivery rule, do
  not repeat it.
- Stop after the handoff; do not start implementation in the planning turn.
- On `go`, execute the preceding plan directly without regenerating it. On a change request,
  revise and present the complete plan again.

## Plan Shape

Write the plan so the next person can act without guessing. Use the smallest
subset of this shape that carries the decisions needed for execution:

```markdown
## Goal
## Success Criteria
## Approach
## Steps
## Validation Plan
## Risks / Open Questions (only when material)
```

Write `None` for open questions only after checking the repo for answers.
Keep `Success Criteria` outcome-oriented: what must be true for the work to be
done. Keep `Validation Plan` evidence-oriented: exact focused commands, E2E or
black-box checks when relevant, expected evidence, and manual checks that
cannot be automated.

Adapt the sections to the plan type:

- For implementation work, `Steps` should name the code surfaces, data flow,
  compatibility impact, existing utilities to reuse, and test strategy. Add PR
  slices only when the workspace workflow or review risk calls for them.
- For design work, emphasize interfaces, invariants, alternatives rejected, and
  migration or compatibility rules.
- For debugging work, list hypotheses, observations needed, instrumentation or
  logs to inspect, reproduction steps, and the evidence that will confirm or
  falsify each hypothesis.
- For rollout or migration work, include phases, gates, rollback, data safety,
  monitoring, and user-visible impact.
- For eval or research work, include the benchmark/question, corpus or sources,
  comparison arms, success metrics, confounders, and reproducibility evidence.

Do not invent an issue, spec, PR, or file path just to fill a section. If the
workspace rules require them, cite the real item or state the missing prerequisite
as an open question or blocker. Do not repeat background the user already knows or
add empty sections. Keep the plan decision-complete enough that an implementer does
not need to invent scope, interfaces, or verification.

## Workflow

1. Classify whether planning is actually needed. If the task is simple AND the
   skill was offered automatically, say so and answer or implement under normal
   rules instead. On an explicit invocation, plan it regardless of size.
2. Complete Research Before Drafting when it applies. Ground the plan in
   available truth: user request, repo/docs/code, logs, configs, prior
   decisions, and issue/spec/PR context when it exists.
3. Identify the plan type and the smallest viable path that proves the approach.
4. Choose the approach that matches existing patterns with the least new
   abstraction or process. Count copied code as new code: when the work is an
   existing component with one behavior changed, copying the component is not
   the low-abstraction choice, and sibling modules that each implement a
   different variant are no precedent for it. Put the difference behind a hook
   the shared code consults; when calls must still dispatch to the new type (so
   a wrapper around the old one would lose the change), make the existing
   implementation generic over a small trait or generate both from one macro.
   Leaving the original untouched, or deferring the sharing to a later
   refactor, is not a reason to copy when existing tests cover the original.
5. Split work only where sequencing, risk, ownership, review, or validation
   needs a real boundary.
6. Map every work unit to validation evidence or a real manual check.
7. If the user or workflow requested a saved plan, briefly report its path. Do not
   announce the absence of a file for the normal inline case.
8. Highlight the highest-risk validation step.
9. Present the plan in the User-Visible Delivery form and stop for the user's
   ordinary next message before implementation.

## Exit

- After generating the plan, present the conversational handoff, the complete canonical
  Markdown, and the repeated handoff in one normal assistant reply. Under the User-Visible
  Delivery exception, reply only as the user asked instead. Under the file-delivery rule,
  reply with the link, verdict and key decisions instead.
- Stop for the user's ordinary next message. Do not treat planning text as permission to edit.
- A follow-up that asks you to review the plan, find its problems, or address them is a
  change request, not a go, even when it asks you to keep going until nothing is left to
  fix. The issues it means are the plan's, and those of any test the user asked for:
  check the plan's claims against the code, correct the plan, and present the revised
  plan with the handoff. A test written to fail until the planned change lands is
  expected to stay red; making it pass is implementation and waits for `go`.
- If the user says go, continue, implement, or otherwise starts execution, use the
  preceding plan directly: leave planning and do the work under the normal workspace
  rules, carrying the plan's structural commitments (see Executing The Plan).
- Re-check the latest user message before editing so stale plan assumptions do
  not override a new instruction.

## Executing The Plan

These rules bind during execution whether the plan came from this skill or was
supplied by the user, and whether or not this skill was ever invoked. If you
loaded this skill at publish time, only this section applies — the planning
restrictions above do not.

- A plan's structural commitments survive into execution: the diff/commit/PR
  split and the unit ordering stay binding while the work is carried out and
  published.
- This governs the shape of publication, never its authorization: [redacted]
  pushing, or publishing still needs the user's ask, per source-control
  safety. A plan step that says "commit" does not by itself authorize a
  commit.
- When the user has you publish work the plan divides into N separate diffs,
  commits, or PRs, publish exactly that split: commit each planned unit
  separately, in the planned order, even when one combined commit would
  satisfy the literal request ("commit this", "publish it").
- Work already finished in one mixed working tree still gets split at publish
  time: group the changed files by plan unit and commit unit by unit. If one
  file's changes span units, split at the hunk level (`git add -p`) or assign
  the file to the earliest unit and say so.

- **Decision-complete**: name the key choices, the recommended choice, and why

## Goal
## Success Criteria

3|description: How to analyse live and past KainBain tasks in production — where task folders live, where every log lives (service logs, deploy log, session transcripts, per-task log entries), and how to inspect a task's state, history, reports, and failure reasons via the filesystem and the live API/WebSocket. 5|---
6|
7|# KainBain Task Analysis (production)
8|
9|This skill teaches an agent how to investigate **live** and **past** KainBain
10|tasks in a production deployment. It covers the two things you almost always
11|need first: **where the task folder is** and **where the logs are**. Everything
12|else is reading those artifacts.
13|
14|KainBain is an AI task orchestrator. Tasks are created into a project's
15|workflow, advance through stages (`agent`, `human`, `ci`, `merge`), and are
16|persisted as markdown on disk. (Legacy `review` stages read as `human`, and
17|legacy `script` / `deploy` stages read as `ci` — a deploy command is an
18|ordinary CI stage now.) Agent stages run on **Runners**: the backend curates
19|the stage prompt and a Runner executes it in a per-task worktree, syncing
20|task docs/assets in and rewriting the backend cwd prefix to the worktree.
21|The API is Fastify; the frontend is served from the same origin. Production
22|is either Docker Compose (`docker compose up -d`, `https://<app-host>`) or a
23|native self-host where the app runs as a systemd **user** service.
24|
25|---
26|
27|## 1. Example deployment profiles (illustrative, optional)
28|
29|| | Dev | Production |
30|| --- | --- | --- |
31|| Repo / project cwd | `{{projectCwd}}` | same repo, but the *deployed* copy is `{{deployDir}}` |
32|| API base | `{{kbApiBase}}` (or `PORT` env) | the public URL / service `PORT` (override `{{kbApiBase}}` — localhost is dev-only) |
33|| Service | none (run manually) | Docker Compose service, or `<service-unit>` (systemd **user** unit on native self-hosts) |
34|| App URL | `{{kbApiBase}}` | `https://<app-host>` |
35|| Task folders | `<project cwd>/docs/tasks/<taskId>/` | same layout, under the project's `cwd` |
36|| Agent execution | embedded (in-process) | Runner worktree (`kb-<taskId>`, cwd prefix retargeted) |
37|
38|**Key fact:** task folders are written under the **project's `cwd`**, not under
39|`{{deployDir}}`. The project's `cwd` is recorded in
40|`<project cwd>/.kainbain/project.json` (e.g. `"cwd": "{{projectCwd}}"`).
41|Tasks live at:
42|
43|```text
44|{{projectCwd}}/docs/tasks/<taskId>/
45|```
46|
47|`{{deployDir}}` is only the *deployed build* (api + frontend/dist + build.json);
48|it does **not** hold task data. Don't look for tasks there.
49|
50|---
51|
52|## 2. The task folder (the single most important artifact)
53|
54|Every task is a directory under `<project cwd>/docs/tasks/<taskId>/`:
55|
56|```text
57|docs/tasks/<taskId>/
58|├── task.md                      # canonical task entity (frontmatter + body)
59|├── IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md       # plan written by the Plan stage (if used)
60|├── plan-<timestamp>.md          # stage report: Plan (only if the stage opted in)
61|├── <stage-slug>-failure-<timestamp>.md  # failure report (ALWAYS written on stage failure)
62|├── automated-tests-<timestamp>.md # CI / human-checkpoint report (always written)
63|└── ...                          # one report per stage run that produced one
64|```
65|
66|**Reporting is opt-in for agent stages.** A default agent stage writes NO
67|report on success — no agent-authored summary file and no engine-generated
68|one. A stage opts in via `report: true` on the stage config or by attaching
69|the `stage-report` skill. Failure reports (`<stage-slug>-failure-<timestamp>.md`)
70|are always written on stage failure, and CI stages (including legacy
71|`script` / `deploy` commands) and merge stages and human checkpoints always
72|write their own reports.
73|
74|### `task.md` — the canonical record
75|
76|`task.md` is the authoritative, server-written snapshot of the task. Read it
77|first. It has YAML frontmatter and a markdown body:
78|
79|- **Frontmatter:** `id`, `projectId`, `workflowId`, `title`, `status`,
80|  `currentStageId`, `createdAt`, `updatedAt`, `enteredStageAt`, `timeInStage`,
81|  `outputReport`, `feedback`, `blockedBy` (plus machine fields such as
82|  `branch`, `reportMetadata`, `timelineMetadata`).
83|- **`# Goal`** — the task's goal/title.
84|- **`# History`** — an append-only audit trail, one line per event:
85|  `- <ISO timestamp>: <action>` (created, edited, stage advanced, failed, etc.).
86|  This is the fastest way to reconstruct what happened and when.
87|- **`# Timeline`** — one line per stage visit (`<timestamp>: <stage> |
88|  <status> | <duration>`, with a diff stat when the stage touched git).
89|- **`# Log Entries`** — the stored per-task log as structured JSON, capped at
90|  `KAINBAIN_LOG_ENTRIES_MAX_COUNT` entries (default 500, oldest evicted under
91|  a marker). This is the single bound on task log storage. (Very old files may
92|  still carry a rendered `# Process Logs` section instead — legacy files are
93|  parsed back into entries on load.)
94|- `KAINBAIN_PROCESS_LOG_MAX_BYTES` (default 32000) only bounds one stage's
95|  captured streamed output kept in memory **while it runs** — it is not the
96|  stored task log.
97|
98|### Stage report files (`<stage-slug>-<timestamp>.md`, `<stage-slug>-failure-<timestamp>.md`)
99|
100|Agent-stage success reports are **opt-in** (stage `report: true` or the
101|`stage-report` skill). Failure reports always exist and carry the `-failure-`
102|filename infix. Auto-generated reports carry the marker
103|`<!-- KAINBAIN AUTO-GENERATED REPORT -->` (hidden in most renderers).
104|A report contains: task, stage type, model, duration, status (PASSED/FAILED),
105|summary of changes, execution output, modified files, and verification status.
106|On failure it includes the error and notes the fallback routing.
107|
108|### `docs/tasks/active/`
109|
110|A separate, manually-maintained scratch area (`docs/tasks/active/<taskId>/N.md`)
111|holds working notes per stage. It is **not** written by the API — treat it as
112|human scratch, not authoritative.
113|
114|---
115|
116|## 3. Where the logs live
117|
118|There are **four** distinct log sources. Match the question to the source.
119|
120|### 3a. Service / request logs — container logs or systemd journal
121|
122|The production API logs Fastify structured JSON (`level`, `time`, `pid`,
123|`req`, `res`, `msg`). Where to read it depends on the deployment shape:
124|
125|```bash
126|# Docker Compose deployment
127|docker compose logs -f backend     # tail live service logs
128|docker compose logs --tail 200 backend
129|docker compose ps                  # confirm the service is up
130|
131|# Native self-host (systemd user unit)
132|journalctl --user -u <service-unit> -f
133|journalctl --user -u <service-unit> -n 200
134|journalctl --user -u <service-unit> --since "2026-10-29 08:00:00"
135|journalctl --user -u <service-unit> -p err -n 100
136|systemctl --user status <service-unit>
137|systemctl --user restart <service-unit>
138|```
139|
140|Use this for: request failures, startup crashes, unhandled errors, and
141|confirming the service is up. On a native self-host the unit file is
142|typically at `~/.config/systemd/user/<service-unit>` (WorkingDirectory
143|`{{deployDir}}/api`, `PORT` set to the API port, `NODE_ENV=production`).
144|
145|### 3b. Deploy logs — `<deploy-state-dir>/`
146|
147|Self-deployment state and logs live under the deploy state directory
148|(typically `~/.kainbain/deploy/` when self-hosting KainBain):
149|
150|```text
151|<deploy-state-dir>/
152|├── deploy.log        # full deploy script output (append-only)
153|├── state.json        # current deploy state
154|├── last-result.json  # last deploy result
155|├── history.jsonl     # append-only deploy history (one JSON per line)
156|├── build.txt         # autoincrementing build counter
157|├── deploy.lock       # flock lock file
158|└── releases/         # per-build release snapshots
159|```
160|
161|The live build number is stamped into `{{deployDir}}/build.json`
162|(`{ buildNumber, deployedAt, commit }`). The header shows `#B<number>` — clicking
163|it opens the KainBain changelog baked into the deploy (`{{deployDir}}/changelog.json`,
164|latest 200 commits on the default branch plus `totalCount`). On Docker
165|deployments the build files live inside the image, not on the host — use the
166|API (`GET /deploy/status`, `GET /deploy/changelog`) instead of host paths.
167|
168|```bash
169|tail -n 200 <deploy-state-dir>/deploy.log
170|cat <deploy-state-dir>/last-result.json
171|cat <deploy-state-dir>/state.json
172|cat {{deployDir}}/build.json
173|```
174|
175|Use this for: "did the deploy succeed / what build is live / why did it roll
176|back". The API also exposes these via `GET /deploy/status`, `GET /deploy/log`,
177|`POST /deploy`, `POST /deploy/rollback`, plus `GET /deploy/changelog` for the
178|baked history (`{ changelog: null, reason: "not-baked" }` before the first
179|deploy that bakes it).
180|
181|### 3c. Agent session transcripts — worktree (Runner) or `.kainbain/sessions/` (embedded)
182|
183|Runner-executed stages keep their session where the harness ran: the
184|per-task worktree on the **Runner host** (`sessionDir` = the worktree), not on
185|the backend. Only embedded (non-Runner) runs write transcripts to the
186|backend's `<project cwd>/.kainbain/sessions/` — one JSONL transcript per
187|session (one JSON object per line): `session`, `model_change`,
188|`thinking_level_change`, and message/tool events, resumed via the SDK's
189|`SessionManager`.
190|
191|```bash
192|ls -lt {{projectCwd}}/.kainbain/sessions/
193|head -5 {{projectCwd}}/.kainbain/sessions/*.jsonl
194|```
195|
196|Use this for: the raw agent conversation / model used / thinking level for a
197|project. Always check **which host ran the stage** first — for Runner tasks
198|the transcript is on the Runner host, and the backend directory may not have
199|it. Note: `.kainbain/` is gitignored, so these are local-only.
200|
201|### 3d. Per-task logs — `# Log Entries` in `task.md`, Live Console on the wire
202|
203|The stored agent/tool/CI output for a task is the `# Log Entries` section of
204|`task.md` (see §2). Live output streams over the WebSocket as `PROCESS_STDOUT`
205|/ `process:stdout` frames, which is what the UI's Live Console renders — for a
206|running task, watch the socket (see §4b), not the file. `task.md` is
207|rewritten on every state change, so its frontmatter, `# History`, and
208|`# Log Entries` stay current, but there is no rendered process-log tail to
209|`tail -f` anymore.
210|
211|---
212|
213|## 4. Analysing a **live** task
214|
215|A "live" task is one currently executing or queued. The engine is a single
216|global executor (`ExecutionQueue`) with an `engineState` snapshot.
217|
218|### 4a. Via the API (fastest, no filesystem)
219|
220|```bash
221|# Engine state: what is running right now
222|curl -s "{{kbApiBase}}/status/observability" | jq '.engine'
223|
224|# Full observability: engine + health + build + task metrics
225|curl -s "{{kbApiBase}}/status/observability?projectId=<projectId>" | jq
226|
227|# Health
228|curl -s "{{kbApiBase}}/status/health" | jq
229|
230|# List tasks for a project (projectId optional → active project)
231|curl -s "{{kbApiBase}}/tasks?projectId=<projectId>" | jq
232|
233|# Single task (full state incl. history, reports, log entries)
234|curl -s "{{kbApiBase}}/tasks/<taskId>?projectId=<projectId>" | jq
235|
236|# Task queue
237|curl -s "{{kbApiBase}}/tasks/queue?projectId=<projectId>" | jq
238|
239|# Session status (active, streaming, message count, disk session)
240|curl -s "{{kbApiBase}}/session/status?projectId=<projectId>" | jq
241|```
242|
243|`GET /status/observability` returns `engine` (status, activeTaskId,
244|activeStageId, activeStageName, activeStageType), `build`, `health`, and
245|`observability` (totals: completed/failed/running/waitingHuman/paused/blocked,
246|plus recent completed/failed lists with failure reasons).
247|
248|### 4b. Via WebSocket (live streaming)
249|
250|The frontend subscribes to `GET /ws?projectId=<projectId>` (WebSocket upgrade).
251|Events are JSON `{ type, sessionId, payload, timestamp }`. Key types:
252|`CONNECTED`, `ENGINE_STATE`, `TASK_UPDATED`, `TASK_DELETED`, `NOTIFICATION`,
253|`PROCESS_STDOUT` / `process:stdout`, and agent events (`agent_start`,
254|`tool_execution_start`, `tool_execution_update`, `tool_execution_end`,
255|`message_update`, `error`). The UI's **Live Console** (Observability dashboard)
256|renders these with severity tags (`AGENT`, `CI`, `ERROR`, `HUMAN`, `TOOL`).
257|
258|To watch live from a script, connect to the WebSocket endpoint at
259|`{{kbApiBase}}/ws?projectId=<id>` (upgrade `http`→`ws` / `https`→`wss`) and log
260|incoming frames.
261|
262|### 4c. Via the filesystem
263|
264|For a live task, `task.md` is rewritten on every state change, so
265|`tail -f docs/tasks/<taskId>/task.md` shows frontmatter, `# History`, and
266|`# Log Entries` growing in near-real-time (watch the WebSocket for the
267|live stream itself — see §3d). The `status` frontmatter tells you where it
268|is: `running_agent`, `running_ci`, `running_merge`, `advancing`, `in_stage`,
269|`waiting_human`, `paused`, `failed`, `completed` (`interrupted` after an
270|unclean restart; `running_deploy` is a legacy label from before the deploy
271|runtime was removed). Note: with Runner execution, absolute backend-cwd paths
272|in prompts are retargeted to the task worktree — resolve worktree-relative
273|paths against `kb-<taskId>`, not the backend checkout.
274|
275|---
276|
277|## 5. Analysing a **past** task
278|
279|A "past" task is one that completed, failed, or was parked. Everything you need
280|is on disk — no live service required.
281|
282|1. **Find the task folder.** List task dirs, newest first:
283|
284|   ```bash
285|   ls -lt {{projectCwd}}/docs/tasks/
286|   ```
287|
288|   Or find by title/status:
289|
290|   ```bash
291|   grep -rl "status: \"failed\"" {{projectCwd}}/docs/tasks/*/task.md
292|   ```
293|
294|2. **Read `task.md`** — frontmatter gives status, current stage, timestamps;
295|   `# History` gives the full event timeline; `# Timeline` gives per-stage
296|   durations; `# Log Entries` gives the stored output.
297|
298|3. **Read the stage reports** in the same folder — one per stage run that
299|   produced one (opt-in agent stages + all failure reports), in
300|   filename-timestamp order. They tell you what each stage produced and
301|   whether it passed or failed. Failure reports use the `-failure-` infix.
302|   For stages that did NOT opt in, reconstruct from `# Log Entries`, the
303|   session transcript (worktree on the Runner host, or `.kainbain/sessions/`
304|   for embedded runs), and the git history.
305|
306|4. **Reconstruct the failure.** For a failed task, check:
307|   - `status: "failed"` in frontmatter.
308|   - The last `# History` entries (e.g. `Stage failed: <reason>`).
309|   - The FAILED stage report (`<stage-slug>-failure-<timestamp>.md`; contains
310|     the error and fallback routing).
311|   - `# Log Entries` tail for the actual error output.
312|   - The API's observability `recentFailed` list (if the service is up) for
313|     `failureReason` / `lastError`.
314|
315|5. **Cross-check the deploy** (if the task reached a deploy command — deploys
316|   run as ordinary CI stages now): see `<deploy-state-dir>/history.jsonl`
317|   and `last-result.json` for whether the deploy succeeded and which build
318|   went live.
319|
320|---
321|
322|## 6. Common analysis recipes
323|
324|### "Why did this task fail?"
325|
326|```bash
327|TASK={{projectCwd}}/docs/tasks/<taskId>
328|grep -E "status|currentStageId" "$TASK/task.md"          # where it ended
329|grep -E "^- " "$TASK/task.md" | tail -20                 # last history events
330|grep -rl "FAILED" "$TASK"/*-failure-*.md                  # failed stage reports
331|grep -E "Log Entries" -A 5 "$TASK/task.md" | tail -20    # stored log tail
332|```
333|
334|### "What is running right now?"
335|
336|```bash
337|curl -s "{{kbApiBase}}/status/observability" | jq '.engine'
338|```
339|
340|### "Did the last deploy work / what build is live?"
341|
342|```bash
343|cat {{deployDir}}/build.json
344|cat <deploy-state-dir>/last-result.json
345|tail -n 50 <deploy-state-dir>/deploy.log
346|```
347|
348|### "What did the agent actually do in stage X?"
349|
350|Read any stage report `<stage-slug>-<timestamp>.md` or
351|`<stage-slug>-failure-<timestamp>.md` (summary, output, modified files) plus
352|the `# Log Entries` section of `task.md`. Agent stages that did not opt into
353|reporting leave no success report — use the session transcript (Runner
354|worktree on the Runner host, or `.kainbain/sessions/` for embedded runs) and
355|git log.
356|
357|### "Is the service healthy?"
358|
359|```bash
360|curl -s "{{kbApiBase}}/status/health" | jq
361|docker compose logs --tail 50 backend          # Docker deployment
362|journalctl --user -u <service-unit> -p err -n 50   # native self-host
363|```
364|
365|---
366|
367|## 7. Gotchas
368|
369|- **Task data is under the project `cwd`, not `{{deployDir}}`.** The deployed
370|  build dir only holds code + `build.json`.
371|- **`task.md` is a snapshot, not a full transcript.** Stored logs are capped
372|  (`KAINBAIN_LOG_ENTRIES_MAX_COUNT`, default 500 entries, oldest evicted under
373|  a marker). For the full agent conversation use the session transcript —
374|  Runner worktree on the Runner host, or the session JSONL in
375|  `.kainbain/sessions/` for embedded runs.
376|- **`.kainbain/` is gitignored** — session transcripts and deploy state are
377|  local-only, not in the repo. Runner worktrees (`kb-<taskId>`) are also
378|  local to the Runner host.
379|- **Absolute backend paths are retargeted on Runners.** The backend curates
380|  prompts with its own project cwd and the Runner rewrites that prefix to
381|  the prepared worktree — a path that exists on the backend may live under
382|  the worktree on the Runner host.
383|- **There is no `deploy` stage type anymore.** Legacy `deploy` (like `script`)
384|  reads as `ci`; merge-plus-deploy composites are migrated into a git-only
385|  merge stage plus a dedicated CI stage. `running_deploy` in old records is a
386|  legacy label.
387|- **`docs/tasks/active/` is human scratch**, not API-written. Don't treat it as
388|  authoritative.
389|- **Auto-generated reports** are marked with
390|  `<!-- KAINBAIN AUTO-GENERATED REPORT -->`; distinguish them from manual ones.
391|- **Agent-stage success reports are opt-in.** A default agent stage that
392|  succeeded leaves NO report file — absence of a `<stage-slug>-<timestamp>.md`
393|  is expected, not data loss. Failure reports (`<stage-slug>-failure-<timestamp>.md`)
394|  are always written.
395|- **The engine is single-threaded** (one global `ExecutionQueue`). Only one
396|  task executes at a time; others queue. `engine.status` is `idle` when nothing
397|  runs.
398|- **Interrupted tasks** (server restart mid-run) are rehydrated with status
399|  `interrupted` and a history entry "Execution recovered after server restart".
400|- **Auto-iteration:** a failed stage may auto re-run (fix → re-test → re-review)
401|  up to `KAINBAIN_MAX_AUTO_ITERATIONS` (default 8) before being parked as
402|  `failed`. Each failed attempt leaves a `<stage-slug>-failure-<timestamp>.md`
403|  report; multiple failure files for the same stage = auto-iteration attempts.

27|## 1. Example deployment profiles (illustrative, optional)
28|
29|| | Dev | Production |
30|| --- | --- | --- |
31|| Repo / project cwd | `{{projectCwd}}` | same repo, but the *deployed* copy is `{{deployDir}}` |
32|| API base | `{{kbApiBase}}` (or `PORT` env) | the public URL / service `PORT` (override `{{kbApiBase}}` — localhost is dev-only) |
33|| Service | none (run manually) | Docker Compose service, or `<service-unit>` (systemd **user** unit on native self-hosts) |
34|| App URL | `{{kbApiBase}}` | `https://<app-host>` |
35|| Task folders | `<project cwd>/docs/tasks/<taskId>/` | same layout, under the project's `cwd` |
36|| Agent execution | embedded (in-process) | Runner worktree (`kb-<taskId>`, cwd prefix retargeted) |
37|
38|**Key fact:** task folders are written under the **project's `cwd`**, not under
39|`{{deployDir}}`. The project's `cwd` is recorded in
40|`<project cwd>/.kainbain/project.json` (e.g. `"cwd": "{{projectCwd}}"`).
41|Tasks live at:
42|
43|```text
44|{{projectCwd}}/docs/tasks/<taskId>/
45|```
46|
47|`{{deployDir}}` is only the *deployed build* (api + frontend/dist + build.json);
48|it does **not** hold task data. Don't look for tasks there.
49|
50|---
51|
52|## 2. The task folder (the single most important artifact)
53|
54|Every task is a directory under `<project cwd>/docs/tasks/<taskId>/`:
55|
56|```text
57|docs/tasks/<taskId>/
58|├── task.md                      # canonical task entity (frontmatter + body)
59|├── IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md       # plan written by the Plan stage (if used)
60|├── plan-<timestamp>.md          # stage report: Plan (only if the stage opted in)
61|├── <stage-slug>-failure-<timestamp>.md  # failure report (ALWAYS written on stage failure)
62|├── automated-tests-<timestamp>.md # CI / human-checkpoint report (always written)
63|└── ...                          # one report per stage run that produced one
64|```
65|
66|**Reporting is opt-in for agent stages.** A default agent stage writes NO
67|report on success — no agent-authored summary file and no engine-generated
68|one. A stage opts in via `report: true` on the stage config or by attaching
69|the `stage-report` skill. Failure reports (`<stage-slug>-failure-<timestamp>.md`)
70|are always written on stage failure, and CI stages (including legacy
71|`script` / `deploy` commands) and merge stages and human checkpoints always
72|write their own reports.
73|
74|### `task.md` — the canonical record
75|
76|`task.md` is the authoritative, server-written snapshot of the task. Read it
77|first. It has YAML frontmatter and a markdown body:
78|
79|- **Frontmatter:** `id`, `projectId`, `workflowId`, `title`, `status`,
80|  `currentStageId`, `createdAt`, `updatedAt`, `enteredStageAt`, `timeInStage`,
81|  `outputReport`, `feedback`, `blockedBy` (plus machine fields such as
82|  `branch`, `reportMetadata`, `timelineMetadata`).
83|- **`# Goal`** — the task's goal/title.
84|- **`# History`** — an append-only audit trail, one line per event:
85|  `- <ISO timestamp>: <action>` (created, edited, stage advanced, failed, etc.).
86|  This is the fastest way to reconstruct what happened and when.
87|- **`# Timeline`** — one line per stage visit (`<timestamp>: <stage> |
88|  <status> | <duration>`, with a diff stat when the stage touched git).
89|- **`# Log Entries`** — the stored per-task log as structured JSON, capped at
90|  `KAINBAIN_LOG_ENTRIES_MAX_COUNT` entries (default 500, oldest evicted under
91|  a marker). This is the single bound on task log storage. (Very old files may
92|  still carry a rendered `# Process Logs` section instead — legacy files are
93|  parsed back into entries on load.)
94|- `KAINBAIN_PROCESS_LOG_MAX_BYTES` (default 32000) only bounds one stage's
95|  captured streamed output kept in memory **while it runs** — it is not the
96|  stored task log.
97|
98|### Stage report files (`<stage-slug>-<timestamp>.md`, `<stage-slug>-failure-<timestamp>.md`)
99|
100|Agent-stage success reports are **opt-in** (stage `report: true` or the
101|`stage-report` skill). Failure reports always exist and carry the `-failure-`
102|filename infix. Auto-generated reports carry the marker
103|`<!-- KAINBAIN AUTO-GENERATED REPORT -->` (hidden in most renderers).
104|A report contains: task, stage type, model, duration, status (PASSED/FAILED),
105|summary of changes, execution output, modified files, and verification status.
106|On failure it includes the error and notes the fallback routing.
107|
108|### `docs/tasks/active/`
109|
110|A separate, manually-maintained scratch area (`docs/tasks/active/<taskId>/N.md`)
111|holds working notes per stage. It is **not** written by the API — treat it as
112|human scratch, not authoritative.
113|
114|---
115|
116|## 3. Where the logs live
117|
118|There are **four** distinct log sources. Match the question to the source.
119|
120|### 3a. Service / request logs — container logs or systemd journal
121|
122|The production API logs Fastify structured JSON (`level`, `time`, `pid`,
123|`req`, `res`, `msg`). Where to read it depends on the deployment shape:
124|
125|```bash
126|# Docker Compose deployment
127|docker compose logs -f backend     # tail live service logs
128|docker compose logs --tail 200 backend
129|docker compose ps                  # confirm the service is up
130|
131|# Native self-host (systemd user unit)
132|journalctl --user -u <service-unit> -f
133|journalctl --user -u <service-unit> -n 200
134|journalctl --user -u <service-unit> --since "2026-10-29 08:00:00"
135|journalctl --user -u <service-unit> -p err -n 100
136|systemctl --user status <service-unit>
137|systemctl --user restart <service-unit>
138|```
139|
140|Use this for: request failures, startup crashes, unhandled errors, and
141|confirming the service is up. On a native self-host the unit file is
142|typically at `~/.config/systemd/user/<service-unit>` (WorkingDirectory
143|`{{deployDir}}/api`, `PORT` set to the API port, `NODE_ENV=production`).
144|
145|### 3b. Deploy logs — `<deploy-state-dir>/`
146|
147|Self-deployment state and logs live under the deploy state directory
148|(typically `~/.kainbain/deploy/` when self-hosting KainBain):
149|
150|```text
151|<deploy-state-dir>/
152|├── deploy.log        # full deploy script output (append-only)
153|├── state.json        # current deploy state
154|├── last-result.json  # last deploy result
155|├── history.jsonl     # append-only deploy history (one JSON per line)
156|├── build.txt         # autoincrementing build counter
157|├── deploy.lock       # flock lock file
158|└── releases/         # per-build release snapshots
159|```
160|
161|The live build number is stamped into `{{deployDir}}/build.json`
162|(`{ buildNumber, deployedAt, commit }`). The header shows `#B<number>` — clicking
163|it opens the KainBain changelog baked into the deploy (`{{deployDir}}/changelog.json`,
164|latest 200 commits on the default branch plus `totalCount`). On Docker
165|deployments the build files live inside the image, not on the host — use the
166|API (`GET /deploy/status`, `GET /deploy/changelog`) instead of host paths.
167|
168|```bash
169|tail -n 200 <deploy-state-dir>/deploy.log
170|cat <deploy-state-dir>/last-result.json
171|cat <deploy-state-dir>/state.json
172|cat {{deployDir}}/build.json
173|```
174|
175|Use this for: "did the deploy succeed / what build is live / why did it roll
176|back". The API also exposes these via `GET /deploy/status`, `GET /deploy/log`,
177|`POST /deploy`, `POST /deploy/rollback`, plus `GET /deploy/changelog` for the
178|baked history (`{ changelog: null, reason: "not-baked" }` before the first
179|deploy that bakes it).
180|
181|### 3c. Agent session transcripts — worktree (Runner) or `.kainbain/sessions/` (embedded)
182|
183|Runner-executed stages keep their session where the harness ran: the
184|per-task worktree on the **Runner host** (`sessionDir` = the worktree), not on
185|the backend. Only embedded (non-Runner) runs write transcripts to the
186|backend's `<project cwd>/.kainbain/sessions/` — one JSONL transcript per
187|session (one JSON object per line): `session`, `model_change`,
188|`thinking_level_change`, and message/tool events, resumed via the SDK's
189|`SessionManager`.
190|
191|```bash
192|ls -lt {{projectCwd}}/.kainbain/sessions/
193|head -5 {{projectCwd}}/.kainbain/sessions/*.jsonl
194|```
195|
196|Use this for: the raw agent conversation / model used / thinking level for a
197|project. Always check **which host ran the stage** first — for Runner tasks
198|the transcript is on the Runner host, and the backend directory may not have
199|it. Note: `.kainbain/` is gitignored, so these are local-only.
200|
201|### 3d. Per-task logs — `# Log Entries` in `task.md`, Live Console on the wire
202|
203|The stored agent/tool/CI output for a task is the `# Log Entries` section of
204|`task.md` (see §2). Live output streams over the WebSocket as `PROCESS_STDOUT`
205|/ `process:stdout` frames, which is what the UI's Live Console renders — for a
206|running task, watch the socket (see §4b), not the file. `task.md` is
207|rewritten on every state change, so its frontmatter, `# History`, and
208|`# Log Entries` stay current, but there is no rendered process-log tail to
209|`tail -f` anymore.
210|
211|---
212|
213|## 4. Analysing a **live** task
214|
215|A "live" task is one currently executing or queued. The engine is a single
216|global executor (`ExecutionQueue`) with an `engineState` snapshot.
217|
218|### 4a. Via the API (fastest, no filesystem)
219|
220|```bash
221|# Engine state: what is running right now
222|curl -s "{{kbApiBase}}/status/observability" | jq '.engine'
223|
224|# Full observability: engine + health + build + task metrics
225|curl -s "{{kbApiBase}}/status/observability?projectId=<projectId>" | jq
226|
227|# Health
228|curl -s "{{kbApiBase}}/status/health" | jq
229|
230|# List tasks for a project (projectId optional → active project)
231|curl -s "{{kbApiBase}}/tasks?projectId=<projectId>" | jq
232|
233|# Single task (full state incl. history, reports, log entries)
234|curl -s "{{kbApiBase}}/tasks/<taskId>?projectId=<projectId>" | jq
235|
236|# Task queue
237|curl -s "{{kbApiBase}}/tasks/queue?projectId=<projectId>" | jq
238|
239|# Session status (active, streaming, message count, disk session)
240|curl -s "{{kbApiBase}}/session/status?projectId=<projectId>" | jq
241|```
242|
243|`GET /status/observability` returns `engine` (status, activeTaskId,
244|activeStageId, activeStageName, activeStageType), `build`, `health`, and
245|`observability` (totals: completed/failed/running/waitingHuman/paused/blocked,
246|plus recent completed/failed lists with failure reasons).
247|
248|### 4b. Via WebSocket (live streaming)
249|
250|The frontend subscribes to `GET /ws?projectId=<projectId>` (WebSocket upgrade).
251|Events are JSON `{ type, sessionId, payload, timestamp }`. Key types:
252|`CONNECTED`, `ENGINE_STATE`, `TASK_UPDATED`, `TASK_DELETED`, `NOTIFICATION`,
253|`PROCESS_STDOUT` / `process:stdout`, and agent events (`agent_start`,
254|`tool_execution_start`, `tool_execution_update`, `tool_execution_end`,
255|`message_update`, `error`). The UI's **Live Console** (Observability dashboard)
256|renders these with severity tags (`AGENT`, `CI`, `ERROR`, `HUMAN`, `TOOL`).
257|
258|To watch live from a script, connect to the WebSocket endpoint at
259|`{{kbApiBase}}/ws?projectId=<id>` (upgrade `http`→`ws` / `https`→`wss`) and log
260|incoming frames.
261|
262|### 4c. Via the filesystem
263|
264|For a live task, `task.md` is rewritten on every state change, so
265|`tail -f docs/tasks/<taskId>/task.md` shows frontmatter, `# History`, and
266|`# Log Entries` growing in near-real-time (watch the WebSocket for the
267|live stream itself — see §3d). The `status` frontmatter tells you where it
268|is: `running_agent`, `running_ci`, `running_merge`, `advancing`, `in_stage`,
269|`waiting_human`, `paused`, `failed`, `completed` (`interrupted` after an
270|unclean restart; `running_deploy` is a legacy label from before the deploy
271|runtime was removed). Note: with Runner execution, absolute backend-cwd paths
272|in prompts are retargeted to the task worktree — resolve worktree-relative
273|paths against `kb-<taskId>`, not the backend checkout.
274|
275|---
276|
277|## 5. Analysing a **past** task
278|
279|A "past" task is one that completed, failed, or was parked. Everything you need
280|is on disk — no live service required.
281|
282|1. **Find the task folder.** List task dirs, newest first:
283|
284|   ```bash
285|   ls -lt {{projectCwd}}/docs/tasks/
286|   ```
287|
288|   Or find by title/status:
289|
290|   ```bash
291|   grep -rl "status: \"failed\"" {{projectCwd}}/docs/tasks/*/task.md
292|   ```
293|
294|2. **Read `task.md`** — frontmatter gives status, current stage, timestamps;
295|   `# History` gives the full event timeline; `# Timeline` gives per-stage
296|   durations; `# Log Entries` gives the stored output.
297|
298|3. **Read the stage reports** in the same folder — one per stage run that
299|   produced one (opt-in agent stages + all failure reports), in
300|   filename-timestamp order. They tell you what each stage produced and
301|   whether it passed or failed. Failure reports use the `-failure-` infix.
302|   For stages that did NOT opt in, reconstruct from `# Log Entries`, the
303|   session transcript (worktree on the Runner host, or `.kainbain/sessions/`
304|   for embedded runs), and the git history.
305|
306|4. **Reconstruct the failure.** For a failed task, check:
307|   - `status: "failed"` in frontmatter.
308|   - The last `# History` entries (e.g. `Stage failed: <reason>`).
309|   - The FAILED stage report (`<stage-slug>-failure-<timestamp>.md`; contains
310|     the error and fallback routing).
311|   - `# Log Entries` tail for the actual error output.
312|   - The API's observability `recentFailed` list (if the service is up) for
313|     `failureReason` / `lastError`.
314|
315|5. **Cross-check the deploy** (if the task reached a deploy command — deploys
316|   run as ordinary CI stages now): see `<deploy-state-dir>/history.jsonl`
317|   and `last-result.json` for whether the deploy succeeded and which build
318|   went live.
319|
320|---
321|
322|## 6. Common analysis recipes
323|
324|### "Why did this task fail?"
325|
326|```bash
327|TASK={{projectCwd}}/docs/tasks/<taskId>
328|grep -E "status|currentStageId" "$TASK/task.md"          # where it ended
329|grep -E "^- " "$TASK/task.md" | tail -20                 # last history events
330|grep -rl "FAILED" "$TASK"/*-failure-*.md                  # failed stage reports
331|grep -E "Log Entries" -A 5 "$TASK/task.md" | tail -20    # stored log tail
332|```
333|
334|### "What is running right now?"
335|
336|```bash
337|curl -s "{{kbApiBase}}/status/observability" | jq '.engine'
338|```
339|
340|### "Did the last deploy work / what build is live?"
341|
342|```bash
343|cat {{deployDir}}/build.json
344|cat <deploy-state-dir>/last-result.json
345|tail -n 50 <deploy-state-dir>/deploy.log
346|```
347|
348|### "What did the agent actually do in stage X?"
349|
350|Read any stage report `<stage-slug>-<timestamp>.md` or
351|`<stage-slug>-failure-<timestamp>.md` (summary, output, modified files) plus
352|the `# Log Entries` section of `task.md`. Agent stages that did not opt into
353|reporting leave no success report — use the session transcript (Runner
354|worktree on the Runner host, or `.kainbain/sessions/` for embedded runs) and
355|git log.
356|
357|### "Is the service healthy?"
358|
359|```bash
360|curl -s "{{kbApiBase}}/status/health" | jq
361|docker compose logs --tail 50 backend          # Docker deployment
362|journalctl --user -u <service-unit> -p err -n 50   # native self-host
363|```
364|
365|---
366|
367|## 7. Gotchas
368|
369|- **Task data is under the project `cwd`, not `{{deployDir}}`.** The deployed
370|  build dir only holds code + `build.json`.
371|- **`task.md` is a snapshot, not a full transcript.** Stored logs are capped
372|  (`KAINBAIN_LOG_ENTRIES_MAX_COUNT`, default 500 entries, oldest evicted under
373|  a marker). For the full agent conversation use the session transcript —
374|  Runner worktree on the Runner host, or the session JSONL in
375|  `.kainbain/sessions/` for embedded runs.
376|- **`.kainbain/` is gitignored** — session transcripts and deploy state are
377|  local-only, not in the repo. Runner worktrees (`kb-<taskId>`) are also
378|  local to the Runner host.
379|- **Absolute backend paths are retargeted on Runners.** The backend curates
380|  prompts with its own project cwd and the Runner rewrites that prefix to
381|  the prepared worktree — a path that exists on the backend may live under
382|  the worktree on the Runner host.
383|- **There is no `deploy` stage type anymore.** Legacy `deploy` (like `script`)
384|  reads as `ci`; merge-plus-deploy composites are migrated into a git-only
385|  merge stage plus a dedicated CI stage. `running_deploy` in old records is a
386|  legacy label.
387|- **`docs/tasks/active/` is human scratch**, not API-written. Don't treat it as
388|  authoritative.
389|- **Auto-generated reports** are marked with
390|  `<!-- KAINBAIN AUTO-GENERATED REPORT -->`; distinguish them from manual ones.
391|- **Agent-stage success reports are opt-in.** A default agent stage that
392|  succeeded leaves NO report file — absence of a `<stage-slug>-<timestamp>.md`
393|  is expected, not data loss. Failure reports (`<stage-slug>-failure-<timestamp>.md`)
394|  are always written.
395|- **The engine is single-threaded** (one global `ExecutionQueue`). Only one
396|  task executes at a time; others queue. `engine.status` is `idle` when nothing
397|  runs.
398|- **Interrupted tasks** (server restart mid-run) are rehydrated with status
399|  `interrupted` and a history entry "Execution recovered after server restart".
400|- **Auto-iteration:** a failed stage may auto re-run (fix → re-test → re-review)
401|  up to `KAINBAIN_MAX_AUTO_ITERATIONS` (default 8) before being parked as
402|  `failed`. Each failed attempt leaves a `<stage-slug>-failure-<timestamp>.md`
403|  report; multiple failure files for the same stage = auto-iteration attempts.

7|# KainBain Task Analysis (production)
8|
9|This skill teaches an agent how to investigate **live** and **past** KainBain
10|tasks in a production deployment. It covers the two things you almost always
11|need first: **where the task folder is** and **where the logs are**. Everything
12|else is reading those artifacts.
13|
14|KainBain is an AI task orchestrator. Tasks are created into a project's
15|workflow, advance through stages (`agent`, `human`, `ci`, `merge`), and are
16|persisted as markdown on disk. (Legacy `review` stages read as `human`, and
17|legacy `script` / `deploy` stages read as `ci` — a deploy command is an
18|ordinary CI stage now.) Agent stages run on **Runners**: the backend curates
19|the stage prompt and a Runner executes it in a per-task worktree, syncing
20|task docs/assets in and rewriting the backend cwd prefix to the worktree.
21|The API is Fastify; the frontend is served from the same origin. Production
22|is either Docker Compose (`docker compose up -d`, `https://<app-host>`) or a
23|native self-host where the app runs as a systemd **user** service.
24|
